summary: Psalm 38 is a plea from a suffering speaker who connects bodily pain, divine displeasure, and his own sin. He describes wounds, weakness, isolation from friends, and enemies who exploit his condition. The psalm moves from confession and silence before attackers to urgent prayer: “Don’t forsake me” and “Hurry to help me.”
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how Psalms can hold guilt, physical anguish, social abandonment, and hope in God in the same prayer. Within Book I, it is one of the David-associated cries where distress does not cancel trust, and trust does not erase distress.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David, for a memorial.” In Psalms, Davidic headings are ancient features of the received collection, but readers differ on whether each heading marks authorship, association, dedication, collection, or later reception.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalms are an anthology formed over centuries; assigning one date to Psalm 38 from this chapter alone would go beyond what can be known here.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, a section dominated by David-associated prayers of distress and confidence. The speaker’s immediate setting is an unnamed crisis involving illness-like suffering, confessed sin, distant companions, and hostile enemies.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic prayer of lament and confession, using compressed images, parallel lines, direct address to God, and a movement from complaint toward urgent petition.

outline.heading: A plea under divine displeasure
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh not to rebuke him in wrath and describes sin and iniquities as overwhelming weight.

outline.heading: Pain throughout the body
outline.note: Wounds, burning, bowed posture, faintness, bruising, and groaning describe the severity of his distress.

outline.heading: God sees what others do not
outline.note: The speaker says his desire and groaning are before the Lord, even as his heart, strength, and eyesight fail.

outline.heading: Friends far off, enemies plotting
outline.note: Loved ones and kinsmen stand at a distance, while enemies lay snares and plan deceit.

outline.heading: Silent before accusation, hopeful before God
outline.note: The speaker does not answer his attackers but places hope in Yahweh and asks that they not gloat when he slips.

outline.heading: Confession amid continuing threat
outline.note: He is near collapse, declares his iniquity, and names enemies who are many and hostile despite his pursuit of good.

outline.heading: Final cry for nearness and help
outline.note: The psalm ends by asking God not to forsake him, not to be far away, and to hurry to help.

keyVerses.text: There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation, neither is there any health in my bones because of my sin.
keyVerses.why: This verse joins bodily suffering, God’s indignation, and the speaker’s sin without explaining the exact cause-and-effect in detail.

keyVerses.text: Lord, all my desire is before you. My groaning is not hidden from you.
keyVerses.why: It anchors the prayer’s trust: even when the speaker is weak and isolated, he believes God sees the whole distress.

keyVerses.text: For I hope in you, Yahweh. You will answer, Lord my God.
keyVerses.why: This is the clearest statement of confidence in the psalm, placed while pain and enemy pressure are still unresolved.

keyVerses.text: Hurry to help me, Lord, my salvation.
keyVerses.why: The final line gathers the chapter into urgent dependence on God for rescue.

questions.question: What is happening to the speaker in this psalm?
questions.answer: The speaker is suffering intensely in body and spirit. He describes wounds, burning, faintness, failing strength, and groaning, while also saying his sin and iniquity weigh on him. The chapter does not give a medical diagnosis or a named event; it presents the crisis as prayer.

questions.question: Does the psalm say all sickness is caused by personal sin?
questions.answer: No. This speaker connects his own suffering with his sin, using phrases like “because of my sin” and “because of my foolishness.” The chapter does not turn that personal confession into a rule for every sufferer. A careful reading should say what this psalm says without making it explain every case of illness.

questions.question: What does “iniquities” mean here?
questions.answer: “Iniquities” is the speaker’s word for his wrongdoing before God. In verse 4, he pictures them as rising over his head and becoming too heavy to carry. In verse 18, he says he will declare his iniquity, so the word belongs to confession, not merely to bad circumstances.

questions.question: Why does the speaker ask God not to rebuke or chasten him?
questions.answer: The psalm opens with a request that Yahweh not deal with him in wrath or hot displeasure. The following verses show why: he feels pierced, pressed down, physically unsound, and overwhelmed by guilt. The prayer does not deny wrongdoing; it asks for mercy within discipline and distress.

questions.question: Why are friends and family standing far away?
questions.answer: Verse 11 says his lovers, friends, and kinsmen stand away from his plague. The psalm does not explain whether they are afraid, repelled, powerless, or socially distancing themselves from his disgrace. What matters in the chapter is the added pain of isolation: those who should be near are not near.

questions.question: Who are the enemies, and what are they doing?
questions.answer: The psalm calls them people who seek his life, seek his hurt, speak mischievous things, and meditate deceits. Later it says they are vigorous, many, and hate him without reason. The chapter does not identify them by name, so they should be read as hostile figures within the poem rather than assigned to a specific episode without more evidence.

questions.question: Why does the speaker stay silent like a deaf or mute man?
questions.answer: Verses 13-14 describe him as not hearing and not opening his mouth. This may show restraint, helplessness, exhaustion, or refusal to answer hostile accusations; readers may emphasize different aspects. The next verse explains the deepest reason for his silence: he is waiting for the Lord to answer.

questions.question: What changes when the speaker says, “For I hope in you”?
questions.answer: The suffering does not disappear after verse 15. He is still ready to fall, still in pain, and still surrounded by enemies. But the direction of the prayer sharpens: instead of answering his attackers, he looks to Yahweh as the one who can answer him.

questions.question: How does the psalm end?
questions.answer: It ends without a report that the pain has lifted or the enemies have left. The last words are urgent requests for God’s nearness and help. That unresolved ending is part of the chapter’s honesty: the speaker is still in need as the prayer closes.

glossary.def: A word in the heading connected with remembering or bringing something before God; the chapter itself begins as a prayer asking Yahweh not to rebuke the speaker in wrath.
Anger or severe displeasure; in verse 1 the speaker asks Yahweh not to rebuke him in wrath.
The speaker’s wrongs or guilt; he says they have gone over his head and are too heavy for him.
Audible or inward expression of distress; the speaker says his groaning is not hidden from God.
Traps; the speaker says those who seek his life lay snares for him.
